# Laravel - Load common header and footer to view

A common pattern in modern web development involves wrapping every page in a shared layout containing navigation, footers, and metadata. In Laravel, this is often achieved using `yield` sections within an `@extends` directive. However, there is a specific scenario where developers need to dynamically select different child views from a controller while maintaining a single master layout. If you attempt to pass the view path as a string variable directly into `View::make()` within a Blade template, the application will throw a "View not found" error, even if the file physically exists on the disk.

The core issue lies in how Laravel interprets the `View` facade versus how it processes Blade directives. The source material demonstrates a scenario where a controller passes `$data['template'] = 'admin/dashboard'` to a view named `common_template`. Inside that view, the developer attempts to resolve the dynamic path using PHP's echo syntax:

```php
<?php echo View::make($template); ?>
```

This approach fails because it bypasses Laravel's Blade compiler. When you use `View::make()` inside a `.blade.php` file with a string variable, Laravel treats that string as a literal path relative to the `views` directory at runtime. However, the error message "View ['admin/dashboard'] not found" suggests a mismatch in how the path is constructed or resolved compared to the static definition used when the code works.

When the developer hardcodes `'admin/dashboard'` directly into the string, it loads successfully. This discrepancy often points to how the data is being scoped or if there are namespace prefixes missing. In the provided example, the controller sets `$template = 'admin/dashboard'`. While this looks correct for a file located in `resources/views/admin/dashboard.blade.php`, the dynamic evaluation inside the Blade template can be fragile if the base path isn't explicitly defined.

The robust solution is to utilize Laravel's native layout inheritance system rather than trying to resolve views dynamically via PHP code strings. Instead of using `View::make()` inside a wrapper, you should extend a master layout file. Create a `layouts/master.blade.php` that includes your header and footer:

```blade
<!-- resources/views/layouts/master.blade.php -->
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head>
    <title>@yield('title')</title>
</head>
<body>
    @include('includes.header')
    
    <main class="container">
        @yield('content')
    </main>

    @include('includes.footer')
</body>
</html>
```

Then, update your controller to extend this layout directly:

```php
namespace App\Http\Controllers;

use Illuminate\Support\Facades\View;

class AdminController extends Controller
{
    public function dashboard()
    {
        $data['title'] = 'Dashboard';
        
        return view('layouts.master', [
            'content' => view('admin.dashboard'), 
            // Alternatively, pass data for the blade file to render directly
            'pageData' => ['title' => 'Dashboard'] 
        ]);
    }
}
```

However, if your architecture requires loading content dynamically without extending a layout, you must ensure the path passed to `View::make()` is an absolute path or correctly relative to the `views` directory. A common pitfall in the original example is that Blade directives like `@include` or `@extends` are compiled before execution, but PHP `echo View::make(...)` runs at runtime. If the variable `$template` contains `'admin/dashboard'`, it expects a file at `resources/views/admin/dashboard.blade.php`.

If you must use dynamic loading inside a Blade template without extending, ensure you are not introducing accidental whitespace or quoting issues that alter the string. The most reliable method remains sticking to `@extends` and `@section('content', view($template))` if you need to pass a pre-loaded view object, though this is less common.

For strictly dynamic content loading where you want to swap views based on controller logic without defining sections in every child, ensure the path passed matches the directory structure exactly. If the file is in `resources/views/admin/dashboard`, the path string must be `'admin.dashboard'` (with dots for directories) or `'admin/dashboard'` depending on your specific Laravel version and configuration conventions. In many versions, dot notation is preferred for subdirectories:

```php
$template = 'admin.dashboard'; // Preferred over slashes in some contexts
```

By aligning the path syntax with Laravel's expectationâusually dot-notation for directory traversalâyou avoid the "View not found" exception when passing variables from controllers to dynamic view loaders.
